author: World Health Organization

text: xiii Why this terminology was developed Traditional medicine has a long history of use in health maintenance and disease prevention and treatment. Ayurveda is one of the most popularly applied health resources throughout the world. According to the second WHO global survey, Ayurveda is a popular form of traditional and complementary medicine in many countries and recognized by several Member States. The development of the WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda is therefore both fundamental and critical to promoting safe and effective Ayurveda health services. Although the needs and demands for traditional, complementary and integrative medicine (TCIM) norms and standards to support training, education, research, health care and information exchange in Ayurveda practice are increasing, work in this area remains weak at the international level. WHO has published benchmarking resources for Ayurveda training and practice, and there is an urgent need to develop standard terminologies to support the use of these documents as well as other Ayurveda technical materials. Based on the needs of Member States, this Ayurveda terminology aims to reduce gaps by providing concise and clear definitions for the essential terms that form the basis of Ayurveda. How was the terminology prepared? The development and completion of WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda took place between 2019 and 2022. The document was prepared with intensive technical support from international experts and related institutions and organizations. The key personnel came from relevant institutions and organizations across the WHO regions and included experts in Ayurveda, other medical systems, medical linguistics and the Sanskrit language. This project was initiated in 2019 by the WHO Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) Unit of the Integrated Health Service Department (IHS). In line with WHO established principles and processes for the development of norms and standards, the TCI Unit drew up the planning proposal and clarified the scope of work. Initially, a task group of international experts scoped for classical literature of Ayurveda included in the syllabi of different levels of Ayurveda training programmes, regulatory requirements for licensure, established national standards and other guidelines available in Member States. They identified 107 classical textbooks of Ayurveda and eighteen web portals to be considered for further assessment. After an initial evaluation, they selected forty-five books and ten web-portals containing terminologies unique to Ayurveda or relevant to its current practice (names of materials, diagnosis, therapeutic interventions, processes, inimitable concepts of Ayurveda and general terms commonly used in Ayurveda literature) for detailed review. The task group also identified and made a separate list of specific terms from general medical literature in the English language which are commonly used in the training and practice of Ayurveda. Based on these, they developed an initial draft comprising 5879 English terms with corresponding terms from the Ayurveda literature Introduction

text: xiii Why this terminology was developed Traditional medicine has a long history of use in health maintenance and disease prevention and treatment. Ayurveda is one of the most popularly applied health resources throughout the world. According to the second WHO global survey, Ayurveda is a popular form of traditional and complementary medicine in many countries and recognized by several Member States. The development of the WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda is therefore both fundamental and critical to promoting safe and effective Ayurveda health services. Although the needs and demands for traditional, complementary and integrative medicine (TCIM) norms and standards to support training, education, research, health care and information exchange in Ayurveda practice are increasing, work in this area remains weak at the international level. WHO has published benchmarking resources for Ayurveda training and practice, and there is an urgent need to develop standard terminologies to support the use of these documents as well as other Ayurveda technical materials. Based on the needs of Member States, this Ayurveda terminology aims to reduce gaps by providing concise and clear definitions for the essential terms that form the basis of Ayurveda. How was the terminology prepared? The development and completion of WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda took place between 2019 and 2022. The document was prepared with intensive technical support from international experts and related institutions and organizations. The key personnel came from relevant institutions and organizations across the WHO regions and included experts in Ayurveda, other medical systems, medical linguistics and the Sanskrit language. This project was initiated in 2019 by the WHO Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) Unit of the Integrated Health Service Department (IHS). In line with WHO established principles and processes for the development of norms and standards, the TCI Unit drew up the planning proposal and clarified the scope of work. Initially, a task group of international experts scoped for classical literature of Ayurveda included in the syllabi of different levels of Ayurveda training programmes, regulatory requirements for licensure, established national standards and other guidelines available in Member States. They identified 107 classical textbooks of Ayurveda and eighteen web portals to be considered for further assessment. After an initial evaluation, they selected forty-five books and ten web-portals containing terminologies unique to Ayurveda or relevant to its current practice (names of materials, diagnosis, therapeutic interventions, processes, inimitable concepts of Ayurveda and general terms commonly used in Ayurveda literature) for detailed review. The task group also identified and made a separate list of specific terms from general medical literature in the English language which are commonly used in the training and practice of Ayurveda. Based on these, they developed an initial draft comprising 5879 English terms with corresponding terms from the Ayurveda literature Introduction WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda xiv in Sanskrit. Descriptions of the terms were prepared based on contextual references from the Ayurveda literature. Each term was given an identification number. In December 2019, the WHO Working Group Meeting on Standard Terminology in Ayurveda was held in IPGTRA, Jamnagar, India. Experts from Austria, Bangladesh, Canada, Denmark, India, Japan, Malaysia, Nepal, New Zealand and Sri Lanka reviewed the draft. The working group examined the draft for the appropriateness of the English terms included in the context of references from the classical texts of Ayurveda. They scrutinized the acceptability of the corresponding Ayurveda terms provided, and the correctness of the Sanskrit script used in the document. The experts also examined the draft for its overall suitability to cover the essential basics of knowledge of Ayurveda, and gave suggestions to categorize the terms and include them in various chapters. A second draft emerged following discussion in the working group and was sent for international peer review. Experts from 18 countries—Argentina, Australia, Bangladesh, Germany, India, Latvia, Malaysia, Mauritius, Nepal, New Zealand, Russian Federation, Singapore, Spain, Sri Lanka, Switzerland, United Republic of Tanzania, United Arab Emirates, and United States of America—covering all six WHO regions, contributed to the peer review. They represented the range of expertise deemed essential in the development of the terminology document and provided suggestions encompassing every aspect of the document, from its overall structural arrangement to specialized technical issues. The peer review inputs were classified as major and minor. Minor suggestions were evaluated, and revisions were undertaken as appropriate within WHO. Major revisions were carried out with technical experts in a series of 26 virtual meetings. The peer-review feedback and revision process led to the development of a third draft. A virtual expert consultation meeting was conducted in October 2021, aiming to conclude the consulting process by inviting experts to finalize the document. A total of 35 experts from Austria, Bangladesh, Canada, Denmark, India, Italy, Japan, Malaysia, Mauritius, Nepal, New Zealand, Sri Lanka, and United States of America, representing the African, American, European, South-East Asian, and Western Pacific regions of WHO, joined the consultation and contributed to the review of the third draft. The meeting reviewed 3876 Ayurveda terms (4012 including synonyms) and made suggestions for developing a fourth draft. The expert consultation meeting unanimously accepted all the suggestions that were made. This meeting marked the conclusion of the technical consultation process, leading to a fourth and final draft for technical editing and publication. What does this terminology cover? A total of 3617 Ayurveda terms (4258 including synonyms) are included in this document, covering: • Background concepts • Core concepts • Structure (anatomical terms) • Morbidity and diagnostic terms (general) • Morbidity and diagnostic terms (diseases/disorders) • Materials • Preparation of medicines

The following key principles were followed in the terminology development process: • Providing a comprehensive definition for all terms included • Use of English as the primary language • Building on related work and following principles relevant to WHO • Upholding the integrity of Ayurveda’s theoretical framework • Keeping definitions concise and clear, and focusing on the core terms in Ayurveda • Making full use of the resources of domestic and international Ayurveda professional bodies, WHO Collaborating Centres for TCIM and the WHO Expert Panel for TCIM. It offers an essential tool and useful reference point for Ayurveda professionals, policymakers, health workers and the general public.

text: Background concepts 11 Term ID English term Description Sanskrit term in IAST* Sanskrit term 1.8.1 Direct perception, observation ITA-1.8.1.1 Direct perception, observation The immediate form of cognition arising from the interaction of the five senses and objects in the world. pratyakṣam प्रत्यक्षम् ITA-1.8.1.2 Contact The process in which the object of cognitive organ(s) (indriyartha),cognitive organ (indriya), mind (manas) and soul (atma) acquire direct perception of an object. sannikarṣaḥ सन्निकर्षः ITA-1.8.1.3 Indeterminate perception Direct perception, observation without specific details of the cognitive process. nirvikalpakam निर्विकल्पकम् ITA-1.8.1.4 Determinate perception Direct perception, observation with specific details of the cognitive process. savikalpakam सविकल्पकम् 1.8.2 Inference based on observations ITA-1.8.2.1 Inference based on observations The process of inference, in which a new conclusion is reached from direct observation by applying reason. anumānam अनुमानम् ITA-1.8.2.2 Inferential knowledge A conclusion reached from stated premises. anumitiḥ अनुमितिः ITA-1.8.2.3 Fallacious reason An argument which appears to be fallacious. ahetuḥ अहेतुः ITA-1.8.2.4 Cause or variable A cause or reason; the immediate cause of an observable event; the pivotal element in the inferential process. hetu हेतु ITA-1.8.2.5 Cause or variable, independent variable A cause possessing all formal characteristics which allow it to act as a sufficient reason for the inference of its marked object; the independent variable influencing the dependent variable. sadhetu सद्हेतु ITA-1.8.2.6 Independent variable Another term for the independent variable. sādhana साधन ITA-1.8.2.7 Dependent variable The effect or dependent variable influenced by the independent variable. sādhya साध्य Chapter 1 WHO international standard terminologies on Ayurveda 12 Term ID English term Description Sanskrit term in IAST* Sanskrit term ITA-1.8.2.8 False positive or false negative A fallacious inference which renders the entire inferential process invalid. hetvābhāsaḥ हेत्वाभासः ITA-1.8.2.9 Invariable concomitance, sensitivity The level of sensitivity between cause (hetu) and sign (linga). When the sign is invariably present with the cause (when the symptom is always seen associated with the pathological condition), this is referred to as invariable concomitance or sensitivity. avinābhāvasaṃbandhaḥ अविनाभावसंबन्धः ITA-1.8.2.10 Non-deviation, specificity The level of specificity between cause (hetu) and sign (linga). When the sign is coterminous with the cause and no other entity (when the symptom is seen only with a particular pathological condition) this is referred to as non-deviation or specificity. avyabhicāritva अव्यभिचारित्व ITA-1.8.2.11 Inseparable coexistence What is inseparable, inherent and essentially unified, e.g. an organic body. ayutasiddhatvam अयुतसिद्धत्वम् ITA-1.8.2.12 Chance effect The chance effect by which a medicine appears to cure or relieve the symptoms of a disease, when it is not possible to confirm a clinical outcome is the result of a given course of action. yadṛcchāsiddhiḥ यदृच्छासिद्धिः ITA-1.8.2.13 Real effect The real and attributable effect of a medicine or treatment, when it is possible to confirm that a clinical outcome is the result of a given course of action. prātiniyamikīsiddhiḥ प्रातिनियमिकीसिद्धिः ITA-1.8.2.14 Conditional effect Relating to or depending on special qualities, limited by particular conditions, valid only under certain suppositions. aupādhika औपाधिक ITA-1.8.2.15 Negative correlation A type of inference in which perception is obtained by negative concomitance (erroneous congruence between two premises). kevalavyatireki- anumānam केवलव्यतिरेकि-अनुमानम् ITA-1.8.2.16 Positive correlation A type of inference in which perception is obtained by positive concomitance (veridical congruence between two premises). kevalānvayi-anumānam केवलान्वयि-अनुमानम् Chapter 1

they are classified into two types depending on their nature. pūrvarūpam पूर्वरूपम् ITA-4.5.2 Classification of prodromes A classification of prodromal symptoms based on their general and specific nature which may indicate a particular disease or condition. pūrvarūpabhedaḥ पूर्वरूपभेदः ITA-4.5.3 Specific prodrome A specific symptom pertaining to a particular dosha. The term also denotes those premonitory symptoms which indicate the onset of a particular disease or clinical condition. viśeṣapūrvarūpam विशेषपूर्वरूपम् ITA-4.5.4 General prodrome General premonitory symptoms. The term also denotes those premonitory symptoms which may indicate the impending disease or condition without providing any information about dosha predominance. sāmānyapūrvarūpam सामान्यपूर्वरूपम् Chapter 4

ITA-4.6.2 Ama, a state of incomplete digestion, transformation or metabolism A transient state of the body wherein the digestive, metabolic processes come to a standstill and do not further transform to end products, by-products or waste products. This standstill leads to various changes in the body such as blockade of channels, excess secretions, unusual accumulation of waste materials, slowing down of movements and catabolic processes. It presents with the following generic symptoms: loss of strength, heaviness, laziness, tastelessness or altered taste, and exhaustion even without physical or mental exertion. The ama phase is an initial stage of almost all disorders, e.g. fever or diarrhoea, which arises due to vitiation of endogenous factors: dosha, fundamental structural components and excretory products. Physiologically, the ama phase denotes early digestion of food in the stomach. āma , āmāvastha आम, आमावस्था ITA-4.6.3 State of active digestion, and transformation of ama An intermediary stage of active digestion and transformation of ama leading to the next non-ama state. This can be a state of natural disease progression or may have to be induced by intervention to mitigate the pathology and treat the condition. Physiologically it is the state of active digestion of food in the intestines. pacyamānāvasthā पच्यमानावस्था ITA-4.6.4 Ripened stage of dosha The transformative phase in the course of a disease or wound indicating a post-inflammatory or suppurative condition. pakvāvasthā पक्वावस्था ITA-4.6.5 Transformative stage devoid of ama pathology The state when ama is converted either under the effect of time or by therapeutic measures. nirāmāvasthā निरामावस्था Chapter 4

title: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda & Charaka Samhita
author: World Health Organization & Maharshi Charaka
licence: Educational & Public Knowledge Reference
locator: Charaka Samhita Chikitsasthana 19 / WHO Atisara Terminology
text: Atisara is the classical Ayurvedic disease category corresponding to diarrhea or excessive watery stool evacuation. According to Charaka Samhita Chikitsasthana Chapter 19, Atisara originates from impaired digestive fire (Agnimandya), ingestion of unwholesome diet, and vitiation of Apana Vayu, Pitta, and Kapha doshas. The vitiated bodily fluids penetrate the digestive tract (Annavaha and Purishavaha Srotas), weakening digestive capacity and resulting in frequent evacuation of liquid feces. Classical Ayurveda categorizes Atisara into six types: Vataja, Pittaja, Kaphaja, Sannipataja, Bhayaja (fear-induced), and Shokaja (grief-induced). Management emphasizes Langhana (lightening therapy), Deepana (stimulating digestive fire), Pachana (metabolizing Ama toxins), Kutaja, Bilva, and oral rehydration using medicated gruels (Peya and Manda).

title: WHO International Standard Terminologies on Ayurveda & Sushruta Samhita
author: World Health Organization & Acharya Sushruta
licence: Educational Reference
text: Trimala refers to the three primary metabolic waste products in classical Ayurveda: Purisha (feces), Mutra (urine), and Sweda (sweat). Sushruta Samhita establishes the foundational principle 'Dosha Dhatu Mala Moolam Hi Shareeram', meaning that Doshas, Dhatus, and Malas constitute the anatomical and physiological foundation of the human body. Malas are not merely discarded substances; while retained for their physiological duration, they provide essential structural support. Purisha supports the colon (Pakwashaya) and stabilizes Apana Vayu. Mutra removes moisture and soluble waste from blood and tissues, maintaining fluid and electrolyte equilibrium. Sweda moisturizes the skin (Twak), regulates body temperature, and supports peripheral hair follicles (Romakupa). Balanced excretion of Trimala is vital for Swasthya (optimal health).

title: Charaka Samhita & Ashtanga Hridaya Dinacharya Regimen
author: Acharya Charaka & Vagbhata
licence: Educational Reference
locator: Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 2 / Charaka Samhita Sutrasthana 5
text: Dinacharya is the comprehensive Ayurvedic daily lifestyle and circadian regimen designed to maintain Dosha balance, prevent disease, and promote longevity. Commencing with waking at Brahma Muhurta (pre-dawn period around 4:00 AM to 5:30 AM), Dinacharya includes natural evacuation, oral hygiene with bitter herbal twigs (Dantadhavana), tongue scraping (Jihwa Nirlekhana), oil pulling (Gandusha and Kavala), herbal collyrium (Anjana), nasal administration of medicated oil (Nasya), full-body warm oil massage (Abhyanga), moderate physical exercise (Vyayama), and bathing (Snana). Adhering to Dinacharya harmonizes biological rhythms with the solar cycle, strengthens sensory organs, enhances vitality (Ojas), and maintains steady Agni.

title: Classical Ayurvedic Seasonal Regimen (Ritucharya)
author: Acharya Charaka & Vagbhata
licence: Educational Reference
locator: Charaka Samhita Sutrasthana 6 / Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana 3
text: Ritucharya represents the Ayurvedic seasonal regimen designed to prevent seasonal aggravation of Tridosha. The solar calendar is divided into two periods: Adana Kala (northern solstice/Uttarayana comprising Shishira, Vasanta, and Grishma), which dehydrates and weakens human physical strength, and Visarga Kala (southern solstice/Dakshinayana comprising Varsha, Sharad, and Hemanta), which imparts strength and nourishment. During Grishma ritu (summer), intense heat depletes Kapha and accumulates Vata while weakening Agni; recommended regimen includes sweet, cooling, liquid foods, milk, coconut water, and rest in shaded environments while avoiding salty, sour, and pungent spices. In Varsha ritu (monsoon), rainwater and environmental dampness aggravate Vata and impair Agni; prescribed regimen includes warm boiled water, aged grains, Deepana-Pachana herbs, and medicated Basti.

title: WHO Benchmarks for Training in Ayurveda & Panchakarma Therapies
author: World Health Organization
licence: WHO Educational & Public Health Guidelines
locator: WHO Benchmarks for Panchakarma / Murddha Taila Procedures
text: Shirodhara is a classical Ayurvedic external purification and rejuvenating therapy belonging to Murddha Taila (cranial oil applications). It involves pouring a gentle, continuous, rhythmic stream of warm medicated herbal oil (Tailadhara), herbal decoction (Kwathadhara), medicated buttermilk (Takradhara), or milk (Ksheeradhara) onto the forehead (specifically the Ajna Marma or third eye region). Shirodhara directly calms Prana Vayu, Sadhaka Pitta, and Tarpaka Kapha, balancing the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. It is extensively used in Ayurvedic practice for relieving stress, mental fatigue, chronic insomnia, tension headaches, anxiety, hypertension, and cognitive exhaustion.

title: Purvakarma Procedures: Snehana and Swedana in Panchakarma
author: Acharya Charaka & Acharya Sushruta
licence: Educational Reference
text: Snehana (oleation therapy) and Swedana (sudation therapy) are the indispensable preparatory procedures (Purvakarma) of Panchakarma. Snehana involves the internal administration of medicated fats (Abhyantara Snehana using medicated ghee or oils) and external application (Bahya Snehana / Abhyanga). Snehana softens tissues, lubricates bodily channels (Srotas), disintegrates Ama toxins, and loosens deep-seated morbid Doshas. Swedana follows Snehana, employing therapeutic heat and induced perspiration (such as steam box / Bashpa Sweda or warm bolus / Nadi Sweda). Swedana dilates microchannels, liquefies the loosened Doshas, and mobilizes them from peripheral tissues (Shakha) into the gastrointestinal tract (Kostha) for safe elimination through Vamana or Virechana.

title: Paschatkarma and Samsarjana Krama in Panchakarma
author: Acharya Charaka
licence: Educational Reference
text: Paschatkarma comprises the post-purification restorative protocols of Panchakarma, primarily centered on Samsarjana Krama (graduated dietetic rehabilitation). Following profound emesis (Vamana) or purgation (Virechana), the patient digestive fire (Agni) is intensely weakened, comparable to a tiny spark of fire. Samsarjana Krama rekindles Agni systematically through a phased liquid-to-solid dietary sequence: beginning with thin rice water (Peya), progressing to thick rice gruel (Vilepi), unseasoned green gram soup (Akrita Yusha), seasoned digestive soup (Krita Yusha), and finally normal wholesome meals. This methodical progression prevents indigestion, restores metabolic enzyme strength, and solidifies cellular immunity.

title: Charaka Samhita Pathology: Rajayakshma and Arshas
author: Maharshi Charaka
licence: Educational Reference
text: Rajayakshma is historically designated as the 'King of Diseases' (Roga Raja) in Charaka Samhita Chikitsasthana Chapter 8, representing a severe condition of systemic tissue depletion (Dhatukshaya) and immune collapse. It arises from four primary causative factors: Sahasa (excessive physical strain beyond capacity), Vegarodha (suppression of natural biological urges), Kshaya (severe grief, tissue depletion, or nutritional loss), and Vishamashana (irregular diet). It manifests with Tri-Rupa (three classic cardinal signs: fever/Jwara, cough/Kasa, and hemoptysis/Raktapitta) or Ekadasha-Rupa (eleven comprehensive systemic signs). Arshas, described in Chikitsasthana Chapter 14, refers to hemorrhoidal polypoid vascular masses in the Guda (anal canal), produced by chronic Mandagni, irregular bowel habits, and vitiation of Apana Vayu.

title: Chyawanprash Rasayana Formulation and Therapeutic Properties
author: Charaka Samhita Chikitsasthana 1.1
licence: Educational Reference
text: Chyawanprash is the premier classical polyherbal Rasayana jam formulation documented in Charaka Samhita Chikitsasthana Chapter 1. Formulated originally for sage Chyawana to restore youth and vitality, its prime ingredient is fresh Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica / Indian gooseberry), processed with Dashamula roots, Pippali, Gokshura, Guduchi, Shatavari, sesame oil, cow ghee, honey, and aromatic spices (Twak, Ela, Tejapatra). Chyawanprash acts as a premier adaptogen, nourishes all seven Dhatus (Sapta Dhatuposhaka), strengthens respiratory immunity (Pranavaha Srotas), rejuvenates lung tissue, improves digestion without aggravating Pitta, and enhances vital life energy (Ojas).

title: Brihat Trayi: The Great Classical Triad of Ayurvedic Literature
author: Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences (CCRAS)
publisher: Ministry of AYUSH, Government of India
licence: Educational Reference
locator: CCRAS Classical History of Ayurveda / Brihat Trayi Overview
text: Brihat Trayi (the 'Great Triad') consists of the three foremost authoritative classical treatises that constitute the canonical foundation of Ayurvedic medicine. 1. Charaka Samhita: Primarily authored by Agnivesha and redacted by Maharshi Charaka and Dridhabala, focusing deeply on internal medicine (Kayachikitsa), etiology, pathology (Nidana), and therapeutics. 2. Sushruta Samhita: Propounded by Divodasa Dhanvantari and compiled by Acharya Sushruta, renowned globally as the foundational classical text on surgery (Shalyatantra), surgical instruments (Yantras and Shastras), anatomical dissection, and reconstructive plastic surgery. 3. Ashtanga Hridaya: Composed in elegant verse by Acharya Vagbhata, synthesizing the core principles of both Charaka and Sushruta into eight clinical branches of Ayurveda in a highly accessible pedagogical structure.

title: Agni Classification: Samagni, Dhatvagni, and Bhutagni in Classical Ayurveda
author: Acharya Charaka & Acharya Sushruta
licence: Educational Reference
locator: Charaka Samhita Grahani Chikitsa 15 / WHO Agni Terminology
text: In classical Ayurveda, Agni represents the complete biological, enzymatic, and metabolic transformation system comprising thirteen distinct varieties. 1. Jatharagni: The primary digestive fire located in the stomach and duodenum (Grahani), governing the four functional functional states: Samagni (equilibrated, ideal digestive power), Vishamagni (erratic fire associated with Vata), Tikshnagni (hyperactive, burning fire associated with Pitta), and Mandagni (hypoactive, sluggish fire associated with Kapha). 2. Bhutagnis: Five elemental metabolic fires corresponding to Parthiva (earth), Apya (water), Tejas (fire), Vayavya (air), and Nabhasa (ether), transforming ingested foods into elemental equivalents. 3. Dhatvagnis: Seven cellular tissue-level metabolic fires responsible for synthesizing and replenishing each specific Dhatu (Rasa, Rakta, Mamsa, Meda, Asthi, Majja, and Shukra). Samagni ensures zero Ama accumulation and radiant Ojas.

title: Dhatuposhana Nyaya: Classical Laws of Tissue Nourishment
author: Acharya Charaka & Chakrapanidatta
licence: Educational Reference
text: Dhatuposhana Nyaya refers to the classical Ayurvedic physiological models explaining the sequence and methodology by which metabolic nutrients (Ahara Rasa) nourish the seven bodily tissues (Sapta Dhatus). Classical commentators describe three complementary Nyayas: 1. Ksheera-Dadhi Nyaya (Law of Direct Transformation / Milk-to-Curd): Postulates that preceding tissues transform completely into successive tissues (Rasa into Rakta, Rakta into Mamsa, and so forth). 2. Kedari-Kulya Nyaya (Law of Irrigation Canal): Postulates that nutrient fluids flow through microchannels (Srotas) like irrigation water through agricultural canals, replenishing each crop/Dhatu in anatomical sequence without complete consumption. 3. Khale-Kapota Nyaya (Law of Selective Uptake / Pigeons in Grain Field): Postulates that specific Dhatus select and extract only their necessary nutritional substrates from circulating plasma according to their cellular receptor affinities.

title: Shad Rasa: The Six Classical Tastes and Dosha Dynamics
author: World Health Organization & Maharshi Charaka
licence: Educational Reference
locator: Charaka Samhita Sutrasthana 26 / WHO Shad Rasa
text: Shad Rasa refers to the six classical dietary tastes identified in Ayurveda: Madhura (sweet), Amla (sour), Lavana (salty), Katu (pungent), Tikta (bitter), and Kashaya (astringent). Each taste arises from a distinct combination of two of the five Mahabhutas: Madhura (Earth + Water), Amla (Earth + Fire), Lavana (Water + Fire), Katu (Fire + Air), Tikta (Air + Ether), and Kashaya (Air + Earth). The tastes exert direct regulatory actions on Tridosha: Madhura, Amla, and Lavana pacify Vata; Tikta, Kashaya, and Madhura pacify Pitta; Katu, Tikta, and Kashaya pacify Kapha. A balanced Ayurvedic meal incorporates all six rasas to nourish all tissues and maintain metabolic stability.

title: Guduchi (Giloy / Tinospora cordifolia) Classical Properties and Pharmacology
author: Central Council for Research in Ayurvedic Sciences & WHO
licence: Educational Reference
locator: Charaka Samhita Sutrasthana 4 / CCRAS Herb Monograph
text: Guduchi (Giloy, Tinospora cordifolia), reverently termed 'Amrita' (immortal nectar) in classical Ayurvedic texts, is among the most versatile Rasayana and Tridoshashamaka herbs. It possesses Tikta (bitter) and Kashaya (astringent) tastes, Ushna (warm) potency, and Madhura Vipaka (sweet post-digestive effect). In classical therapeutics, Guduchi is the primary medicinal drug for Jwara (fever, particularly chronic and recurrent fevers), Deepana-Pachana (burning Ama toxins), Prameha (diabetes and metabolic syndromes), and Kushtha (skin disorders). Contemporary phytochemical research confirms its potent immunomodulatory, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and hepatoprotective properties.
